top_cited_works.title: Amine–Boranes: Green Hypergolic Fuels with Consistently Low Ignition Delays
top_cited_works.abstract: Complexation of amines with borane converts them to hypergols or decreases their ignition delays (IDs) multifold (with white fuming nitric acid as the oxidant). With consistently low IDs, amine-boranes represent a class of compounds that can be promising alternatives to toxic hydrazine and its derivatives as propellants. A structure-hypergolicity relationship study reveals the necessary features for the low ID.

recent_works.title: An Alternate Mechanism for the Reactions of Methylhydrazine with Dinitrogen Tetroxide
recent_works.abstract: Various mechanisms have been proposed in the literature for the hypergolic reactions of methylhydrazine (MMH) and dinitrogen tetroxide (NTO). Most of these mechanisms involve radical reactions. However, experimental results obtained on the liquid-phase reactions of MMH and NTO by using high-resolution linear quadrupole ion trap/orbitrap mass spectrometry suggest that highly energetic ionic reactions play an important role in the hypergolic reactions of MMH with NTO. The elemental compositions of the detected ions were determined and their structures were explored by using tandem mass spectrometry experiments. Quantum chemical calculations indicate that the reactions of the nitrosonium and/or nitronium cations generated from NTO via the unsymmetrical NTO (UNTO) are important in explaining the hypergolic behavior of NTO with MMH. The most important reactions include the initial generation of the MMH radical cation that then reacts with the nitrate anion or nitrogen dioxide radical to form the final detected product ions.

recent_works.title: KHz rate 3D white light particle tracking with a tunable acoustic gradient (TAG) lens
recent_works.abstract: This work develops a 70 kHz tunable acoustic gradient (TAG) lens and high-speed camera configuration for three-dimensional diagnostics of multiphase particle flows. The experimental scene is back-illuminated with a pulsed LED, driven by custom hardware, to capture images with variable phase delays with respect to the sinusoidal TAG lens focal sweep. Proposed calibration methodology and data processing techniques automate the 3D localization and tracking of particles recorded by this configuration. Capabilities are quantitatively assessed by investigating the conically expanding particle field produced by a vibrating nozzle, and good agreement between the statistics of the velocity components demonstrates comparable accuracy in the in-plane and optical depth directions. Finally, capabilities are demonstrated for a challenging and practical measurement of hypergolic reaction of nitrogen tetroxide (NTO) and monomethylhydrazine (MMH). TAG recordings are shown to provide finer depth resolution and reduced susceptibility to imaging noise compared to the common digital inline holography (DIH) diagnostic. recent_works.title: Design and Performance Analysis of an Optically Accessible Pneumatic Poppet Valve
recent_works.abstract: This paper discusses the design and testing of an optically accessible pneumatic poppet valve. In a graduate-level course titled “Propulsion Design Build Test” at Purdue University, students were tasked with designing optically accessible components for a hypergolic rocket engine experiment. As a part of this class, we designed this valve to study actuation dynamics and sealing characteristics and to gain greater insight into operational aspects of poppet valves, a common type of valve used in aerospace systems. The team designed the value to nominally operate at 500 psia with materials that are compatible with high-test peroxide. We used polycarbonate to make the valve’s casing, actuation stem, and poppet, which allowed for optical accessibility into the valve. The valve uses a hard-on-soft cone-on-cone poppet and seat configuration. The team designed the poppet and seat as modular components, enabling testing of different configurations and quick design iteration. As part of the designing process, we performed an analysis to estimate the actuation time and force margin of the valve as defined by NASA STD-5017. recent_works.title: Development of an Optically Accessible Green Hypergolic Rocket Engine with Bi Swirl Injector
recent_works.abstract: This work aims to investigate the flow and ignition dynamics of hypergolic propellants by designing, fabricating, and testing a bipropellant thruster that incorporates direct optical access throughout the entire system. Unlike conventional thrusters, the presented design integrates a transparent chamber, injector, and fluid components, enabling unobstructed visualization of the complex phenomena occurring during propellant injection, mixing, and combustion. Optical access provides a unique diagnostic capability, allowing researchers to employ high-speed imaging, laser-based techniques, and spectroscopy to capture transient ignition events, flame structure evolution, and flow-field interactions. These insights are critical for advancing the fundamental understanding of hypergolic ignition chemistry and fluid dynamics, ultimately informing the development of safer, more reliable, and more efficient propulsion systems. recent_works.title: Experimental and Numerical Study of an Optically Accessible Cavitating Venturi
recent_works.abstract: Cavitating venturis are flow metering devices that exploit an inherently unstable phenomenon, which is challenging to model accurately. To improve understanding of venturi performance, it is essential to visualize the cavitation structure. In a graduate-level course titled “Propulsion Design Build Test” at Purdue University, students were tasked with designing optically accessible components for a hypergolic rocket engine experiment. We designed a pressure vessel rated for 500 psig and incorporated a transparent body manufactured via stereolithography using Formlabs V4.1 resin. This printed body was secured between the vessel’s endcaps and featured an axisymmetric conical converging-diverging flow path. We analyzed the venturi’s surface roughness using optical profilometry and found it significantly higher than typical machining roughness for metal, which influences cavitation behavior. To capture the cavitation phenomenon, we employed high-speed cameras with microsecond exposure, achieving high-resolution visualization across a range of inlet pressures.
